The wrong pair is (2) Ramman - Dance form in West Bengal.

The chapter's list of Indian traditions declared as Oral and Intangible heritage states that Ramman is a religious festival and ritual theatre of the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, declared in 2009. So this pair is wrong on both counts: Ramman is not a dance form, and it does not belong to West Bengal. In the chapter's list, West Bengal is mentioned for the Chhau dance (West Bengal, Jharkhand, Odisha), not for Ramman.

The other three pairs agree with the chapter. Kootiyattam is Sanskrit theatre of Kerala (2001), Ramlila is the traditional performance of the Ramayana (2005), and Kalbelia is the folk songs and dances of Rajasthan (2010).

[Note: the chapter's own list places Ramlila in 'North India', while the exercise prints 'Uttar Pradesh'. Uttar Pradesh is named nowhere in the chapter's heritage lists; it occurs only in this exercise question itself. Pair (3) is still not the wrong pair, because it only narrows the wider region the chapter gives, whereas pair (2) contradicts the chapter on both the description and the State.]

Applied History is also known as 'Public History'. It is a field of study concerned with the application of history for the benefit of people in contemporary and future times. Knowledge of history is useful because it can give guidance in finding solutions to present-day social issues and in incorporating those solutions into social planning. Projects and programmes related to applied history create opportunities for ordinary people to take part along with technical experts, and people also take part as tourists visiting museums and ancient sites, which creates interest in history. In short, applied history means understanding our present with the help of history and finding the right direction for the benefit of our future.

Archives preserve and store old documents, official records, old films and similar material. The National Archives of India is in New Delhi, and every state in India maintains its own archives independently. Some archives are set up for a distinct purpose. The main office of the National Film Archives of India is in Pune, Maharashtra; it was established in 1964 as the Media Unit of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting of the Indian Government. It served three objectives: to search for and obtain rare Indian films and preserve this heritage for future generations, to categorise the important aspects of films by creating documentation and catalogues and carrying out research, and to establish a centre for the dissemination of 'films culture'. The chapter also lists Museums and Archives as one of the professional fields affiliated to applied history, needing trained archive management professionals.

Cultural heritage is in the form of human creation, and it is of two types - tangible and intangible.

| Cultural Heritage | Items included (as given in the chapter) |
|---|---|
| Tangible | Ancient sites, buildings, artefacts (the chapter also lists manuscripts, sculptures and paintings) |
| Intangible | Oral traditions and their language, traditional knowledge, social customs and rituals of celebrating festivals (the chapter also lists styles of performing arts, certain traditional skills, and the communities or groups who represent such traditions, customs and skills) |

The concept map asks for three items in each branch. The chapter supplies more than three for each type, so any three from the lists above may be written in the blanks.

It is essential to study the history of technology because it helps us understand the changes that took place in fields such as agricultural production, commodity production, architecture and engineering, and also the causes of those changes. Scientific discoveries and inventions on one side and technological advancement on the other are mutually dependent on each other, so neither can be understood alone. Knowledge of science and technology was important at every step in the evolution of mankind, from the making of stone tools to agricultural production. Later, the advancement of science promoted the mechanisation of production. Therefore the history of technology has to be known in order to understand how mechanisation developed and how science and technology depend on each other.

It is essential for the benefit of future generations to preserve our heritage. UNESCO is the global organisation that has announced certain directives with the objective of promoting cultural and natural heritage. On the basis of those directives, sites and traditions are declared as 'World Heritage', and so the list of World Heritage Sites is announced by UNESCO. The chapter gives lists of Indian entries under three headings - traditions declared as Oral and Intangible heritage, World Cultural Heritage Sites and World Natural Heritage Sites. For example, the Western Ghats are now included in UNESCO's list of World Natural Heritage, and the Kaas plateau in Satara district is a part of the Western Ghats.

Our present way of life has been shaped by a historical chain of events, and every field of knowledge has its own history of development. The direction of future development in any field depends on the state of knowledge already available in it. That is why the method of history is of value in research in various fields.

(a) Science: The history of science helps in understanding the chronological order of scientific discoveries, inventions and theories. It also helps us understand the cause-effect chain that led to those discoveries and inventions. It is said that 'need' is the mother of inventions; discoveries and inventions are often the result of human efforts to fulfil a need and also of curiosity, and these efforts are based on scientific knowledge that is already available. So knowledge of the history of science helps in understanding both the factors that facilitated a discovery or invention and its chronology.

(b) Arts: It is important to understand how various art forms developed, with the help of their style of expression and their foundation in intellectual, emotional and cultural traditions. The key to the expressions in any art form, the emotional temperament of the artist, and the developmental history of that art form can all be understood with the help of cultural history.

(c) Management Studies: To understand the various factors in the chain of production - the means of production, human resources and the processes of production - and also the chain of market and sales management, it is essential to know how similar functional systems worked in the past. Healthy management also requires an understanding of the psychological character of the people working at various levels in the chain of production and marketing, and for that an understanding of the social and economic institutions supporting industrial and commercial processes is important. Knowledge of history in this regard makes management at various levels easier.

People often ask what the practical value of history is, and applied history is the answer to that question. The visible and invisible relics of the past exist in our present, and we feel curiosity and attraction towards them. We wish to know more about their history because they represent the creative thoughts and traditions of our ancestors. They are our heritage, and heritage helps in building our identity, because the history of our heritage links us with our origin. It therefore becomes necessary to preserve and conserve that heritage for the future, for our own benefit as well as for the benefit of coming generations. Applied history is concerned with this preservation and conservation and with making our heritage accessible to people, and heritage management also creates opportunities of employment. Applied history further gives guidance in finding solutions to present social issues and in incorporating them into social planning. In brief, applied history is the understanding of our present with the help of history and the finding of the right direction for the benefit of our future.

The chapter suggests the following measures for the preservation of the sources of history:

(1) Preserve and conserve our heritage for the future, for our own benefit as well as for the benefit of future generations, since this is one of the main concerns of applied history.

(2) Carry out the work of conservation and preservation of cultural heritage through the responsible authorities, namely the Archaeological Survey of India and India's State Departments of Archaeology.

(3) Support organisations such as INTACH (Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage), which is actively working in this field.

(4) Involve experts from various fields in conservation and preservation work, and make sure they are duly aware of the cultural, social and political histories of the heritage site.

(5) Handle all the operations necessary for the conservation, preservation and development of a heritage site without causing any change in its original state.

(6) Survey in detail the local social structure, the psychology of the local people, the challenges they face in present situations and their expectations, before taking up a project.

(7) Take due precautions to avoid hurting the sentiments of the local people while completing a project of conservation, preservation and development.

(8) Facilitate the participation of local people in such projects, and encourage people to volunteer in the conservation and preservation projects of their own city, town or village.

(9) Design a systematic plan to employ local skills in a creative way and create better opportunities of livelihood, so that people have a stake in preserving the heritage.

(10) Follow the directives announced by UNESCO for promoting cultural and natural heritage, on the basis of which sites and traditions are declared as 'World Heritage'.

(11) Maintain museums and archives, which preserve and store old documents, official records and old films, as the National Archives of India and the state archives do, and as the National Film Archives of India does for rare Indian films.

(12) Conduct public training programmes and create social awareness about the conservation and preservation of our cultural and natural heritage, and strictly avoid the vandalising of historic and public places so that they are preserved for future generations.

Tourism also helps, because visiting museums and ancient sites creates interest in history among people and draws them into conservation work.

Cultural and Natural Heritage Management is one of the main aspects of applied history, and the following objectives can be fulfilled through heritage projects.

(1) The operations necessary for the conservation, preservation and development of a heritage site can be handled without causing any change in its original state.

(2) The local social structure and the psychology of the local people, the challenges they face in the present situation and their expectations can be surveyed in detail.

(3) Due precautions can be taken to avoid hurting the sentiments of the local people while the work of conservation, preservation and development is being completed.

(4) The participation of the local people in the project can be facilitated.

(5) A systematic plan can be designed to employ local skills in a creative way and to create better opportunities of livelihood.

Besides these, heritage management creates opportunities of employment for specialised experts such as architects, engineers, historians, archaeologists, museum curators, sociologists, archive management professionals, legal experts and skilled photographers. Heritage projects also help in creating social awareness about the conservation and preservation of our cultural and natural heritage, in enhancing the professional skills of people, in developing the industrial and commercial field, and in ensuring that historic and public places are not vandalised but preserved for the benefit of future generations.
